title: Transformers with Endogenous In-Context Learning: Bias Characterization and Mitigation
claim: Pretrained models trained on confounded data show systematic, strength-dependent deviation in learned representations, empirically confirming the theoretical prediction of bias.
layout: 4 line-plot panels in a row, shared Iteration x-axis, dual y-axes in (a-b)
description: A single row of four line plots, each with training iteration on the x-axis and captions (a) to (d) beneath. Panels (a) and (b) track the 3rd layer of a 3-layer transformer and the 1st layer of a 1-layer transformer. Each has a left axis for cosine divergence and a right log-scale axis for L2 divergence and prediction divergence. Green, purple or red, and black or brown curves with shaded bands show cosine divergence jumping early and then plateauing. L2 and prediction divergence drop quickly and stay flat. Panels (c) and (d) plot the parameter difference of the 3rd-layer dimension against iteration for four confounding strengths, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0. The curves are blue, orange, green and red, with error bars. Stronger confounding generally gives larger deviation. The eye goes first to the colored curves and legends.
caption: (a-b): Verification of Lemma 1; (c-d): Deviation of Pretrained Weights in Theorem 1.
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables pre-trained transformers (TFs) to perform few-shot learning across diverse tasks, fostering growing research into its underlying mechanisms. However, existing studies typically assume a causally-sufficient regime, overlooking spurious correlations and prediction bias introduced by hidden confounders (HCs). As HC commonly exists in real-world cases, current ICL understandings may not align with actual data structures. To fill this gap, we contribute the pioneer theoretical analysis towards a novel problem setup termed as ICL-HC, which offers understanding the effect of HC on the pre-training of TFs and the following ICL prediction. Our theoretical results entail that pre-trained TFs exhibits certain prediction bias with proportional to the confounding strength. To migrate such prediction bias, we further propose a gradient-free debiasing method named Double-Debiasing (DDbias) by collecting and prompting with extremely few unconfounded examples, correcting pre-trained TFs with unbiased ICL predictions. Extensive experiments on regression tasks across diverse designs of the TF architectures and data generation protocols verify both our theoretical results and the effectiveness of the proposed DDbias method.
